turns:
=== CALL C0523 ===
Bethany: Hi. Erm, hello. Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah, fine. Hi.
Bethany: Hi. Sorry, I'm Bethany.
Craig: Craig.
Bethany: ...
Craig: So. Three minutes, yeah?
Bethany: Yeah, I think so. I wasn't sure if we're meant to talk about anything in particular.
Craig: Don't think so. Just chat, I reckon. How'd you get on with the puzzle thing?
Bethany: Erm, not very well, to be honest. I got stuck on the one with the shapes, the rotating ones, and sort of gave up on it in the end.
Craig: Yeah, that one was a bit daft. I just guessed most of them.
Bethany: Oh, that makes me feel a bit better, thanks.
Craig: Where are you, then?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Craig: Right. Never been. Stevenage, me.
Bethany: Oh, okay. Is that near London?
Craig: Sort of. Half an hour on the train. It's fine, yeah. Nothing much there.
Bethany: What do you do? If that's... sorry, if that's okay to ask.
Craig: Yeah, course. Software developer. Back-end stuff, for a logistics company. Basically we write the systems warehouses use, so stock, picking, which lorry goes where, that sort of thing. I mostly work from home, so it's me in the box room all day with the headphones on. Pretty boring to explain, honestly.
Bethany: No, that's quite interesting actually. My boyfriend works in a warehouse. He drives a forklift at a distribution centre off the M5. They've got a system that tells him where to go on a little screen, I think.
Craig: Yeah, that'll be something like ours. Probably not ours, but similar. Does he moan about it?
Bethany: Erm... a bit. He says it freezes sometimes and they all just have to stand around.
Craig: Yeah, that's usually somebody on the back end. Could be me, to be fair.
Bethany: I won't tell him.
Craig: Cheers. What about you, what do you do?
Bethany: Erm, I'm sort of... I'm looking for work at the moment. I did a packing job but it was seasonal, so it ended. I volunteer at a charity shop two mornings a week, the hospice one. So, yeah.
Craig: Fair enough.
Bethany: ...
Craig: Is that your drawing behind you? The bird.
Bethany: Oh, yeah. It's a robin. I draw quite a lot, mostly birds and plants. There's a little egret that's been down by the river this week, so I've been trying to get that, but they don't keep still. They stand dead still for ages and then just go, and you've only got half a leg.
Craig: Half a leg. Yeah, that robin's decent though. Looks proper.
Bethany: Thank you. That's kind.
Craig: You sell them or anything?
Bethany: No, not really. I put some on Instagram. I've got a few hundred followers, which isn't much. I'd like to do commissions maybe, one day, but I'm not sure I'm good enough yet.
Craig: Few hundred's more than I've got. I'd just charge people. Honestly, half of getting paid is just asking for it. I've moved jobs twice 'cause I asked for more money and they said no.
Bethany: I think I'd be too scared to ask.
Craig: Yeah, most people are. That's why they don't get it.
Bethany: Mm. Maybe. Is that a bike behind you? In the corner.
Craig: Yeah. Road bike. Bought it in lockdown, cost way too much. I ride it about four times a year. Needs a service, I've been saying that for about a year.
Bethany: We walk mostly. On the Levels, and up the Quantocks sometimes if Kieran drives us.
Craig: Is that hills?
Bethany: Yeah, sort of... they're not huge, but it's really nice at the top. You can see right over to Wales on a clear day.
Craig: I'd probably cycle it if it was flat.
Bethany: The Levels are flat. Very flat. That's kind of the whole point of them.
Craig: Go on then, maybe I'll stick the bike on the—

=== CALL C0524 ===
Gemma: Right. Hi. Can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah. Hi. Craig.
Gemma: Gemma. Funny, my husband's called Craig.
Craig: Lot of us about.
Gemma: Mm. So what is this, we just talk for three minutes and that's it?
Craig: Pretty much. Did one already. Goes quick.
Gemma: Good. I've been on since six, I'm knackered.
Craig: What do you do, then?
Gemma: Site ops manager. Distribution centre up near Alconbury, third-party logistics. About a hundred and eighty staff over three shifts. So basically if a trailer doesn't turn up or the agency don't send enough bodies, it's my phone that goes. Had a client on at me at seven this morning about peak volumes. Peak's a nightmare every year, without fail.
Craig: Huh. I write warehouse software. Logistics company in Cambridge.
Gemma: You're joking.
Craig: Back-end. The bit that works out allocation, picking routes, that sort of thing.
Gemma: Which one?
Craig: Probably not one you'd know. Mid-sized.
Gemma: Well, whoever does ours wants shooting. It goes down every time we hit volume. Every time. Two hundred people stood there with scanners going "Gem, it's frozen again."
Craig: Yeah, that's usually not the software, to be fair.
Gemma: Course it's not.
Craig: No, honestly. Nine times out of ten someone's set it up badly on site. Waves configured wrong, or the server's some ten-year-old box in a comms cupboard. Then they ring us and it's our fault. Had one last month, their whole system was running off a server someone had put a kettle next to.
Gemma: A kettle.
Craig: Steam. In the cupboard. For about two years.
Gemma: ...That's actually quite funny. That'd be my lot an' all, to be honest.
Craig: It's always somebody's lot.
Gemma: Do you go out on site, then, or?
Craig: God, no. Home, mostly. Office once a fortnight.
Gemma: Must be nice. Sat at home in your joggers.
Craig: It's alright, yeah.
Gemma: I'd go mad. I'd also never answer an email again, so. My inbox is about four thousand.
Craig: Four thousand?
Gemma: Ish. My deputy does the important ones, Priya. She's the only reason that place runs, honestly. Don't tell her I said that.
Craig: I'm not gonna meet her.
Gemma: No. Good. ...Cambridge, though, so you're on the A14?
Craig: A1(M). Which is a nightmare.
Gemma: Try the A14. The roadworks. I've spent more time sat by Girton this month than I have at home.
Craig: Yeah, I avoid it.
Gemma: Lucky you. ...Them headphones. You were on a game before this, weren't you?
Craig: Bit. Lunch break.
Gemma: It's gone four.
Craig: Flexible hours.
Gemma: Flexible. Right. If one of my team leaders said that to me I'd have them in the office.
Craig: Good job I don't work for you, then.
Gemma: Yeah, it is, mate. You'd last about a week. My Craig's the same, mind, he's Arsenal, been in a mood since Sunday—
Craig: Oh, don't. They bottled it agai—

=== CALL C0525 ===
Chloe: Hiya! Oh, sorry, hi. Can you hear me okay?
Bethany: Yeah. Hi. I'm Bethany.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous, I don't know why, it's only three minutes.
Bethany: No, me too. I've done one already and I still am.
Chloe: Oh, how was it?
Bethany: It was okay. He was nice, sort of. He just didn't say loads. Well, he did, but... I'm not sure really.
Chloe: Oh, I think I know who you mean, from the photos. Erm. Where are you from?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Chloe: Oh, nice. I'm in Bloxwich, which is Walsall, kind of near Birmingham. Probably means nothing to you.
Bethany: Not really, sorry.
Chloe: No, that's fine, it doesn't mean much to anyone! What do you do?
Bethany: I'm looking for work at the moment. I volunteer in a charity shop, the hospice one. What about you?
Chloe: I'm at uni, third year, primary teaching. So I'm about to do my last placement, which I'm kind of terrified about, to be honest. I've done Year 2 and Year 4, and the kids were lovely, it's not the kids. It's more the staff room. Everyone's been there twenty years and they all know where they sit, and you're stood there with your mug like, can I... is this anyone's chair? Sorry, I'm rambling.
Bethany: No, you're not. I'd be scared of the staff room too.
Chloe: It's the worst bit! Honestly, give me thirty six-year-olds any day.
Bethany: Are those picture books behind you?
Chloe: Yeah! I've been collecting them for my classroom, like, when I get one. Some of them are from charity shops, actually. The illustrations in some of them are just gorgeous, the kids stare at them for ages.
Bethany: I love picture books. I sort of draw, a bit. Birds, mostly.
Chloe: Oh, was that your robin? In your photo? I thought that was lovely.
Bethany: Oh. Yeah, that was mine. Thank you. I do pencil and fineliner, mostly what I see by the river or out on the Levels. I'd love to illustrate a nature book one day. Like a proper one, with all the birds in. But I don't know, I'm not really... I'm not sure I'm good enough to call myself an artist. Sorry, that's a bit much.
Chloe: No, it's not! You totally should. Kids would love that. They go mad for birds, honestly. We did a birdwatch in Year 2 and one boy cried because he saw a blue tit.
Bethany: Aw. That's really sweet.
Chloe: He was so happy. Erm, yeah. That's it really.
Bethany: ...
Chloe: Sorry, what else do you like doing?
Bethany: Reading. Walking. And I bake when I can't sleep. I made flapjacks at about two this morning.
Chloe: Oh my God, same. I bake when I'm stressed. I'm doing banana bread tonight for placement prep, but I've got to wait until my mum's done tea.
Bethany: I do banana bread too! Kieran says he's sick of it.
Chloe: Kieran? My brother's called Kieran! He's seventeen, he eats all the crisps.
Bethany: Mine's my boyfriend. He's on nights this week, so it's just me and the smell of chips from downstairs.
Chloe: Chips?
Bethany: We live above a takeaway. It's sort of nice, sometimes, and sometimes it's—

=== CALL C0526 ===
Darren: Alright! There she is. Can you hear me, love?
Gemma: Yeah. Gemma.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you. Third one of these for me, I'm getting good at it now.
Gemma: Same. Is this the last one?
Darren: Dunno, mate. I just do what the screen tells me.
Gemma: Fair enough. Where are you?
Darren: Bridgwater, Somerset. Born and bred. You?
Gemma: Huntingdon. Cambridgeshire.
Darren: Never been. Is it nice?
Gemma: It's alright. It's got a Tesco.
Darren: Ha! Sold me. So what do you do, then? You look like you've come straight from work, with the fleece.
Gemma: Yeah, I have. Site ops manager at a distribution centre. Warehouse, basically. About a hundred and eighty staff.
Darren: No way. I was on forklifts, me. Distribution centre off the M5, years. Counterbalance mostly.
Gemma: Yeah? Where are you now, then?
Darren: Er, nowhere at the minute. Did my back in. Signed off about eighteen months ago, so I'm on the Universal Credit, seeing a work coach every couple of weeks, the whole lot. Looking at lighter stuff, van driving maybe, or caretaker at a school. Not much call for a forklift driver who can't twist round, do you know what I mean?
Gemma: Mm. You could do a lot worse than security. We're always short of gatehouse.
Darren: Yeah, that's on the list.
Gemma: Get your CV in early, though, don't wait for it to come to you. I've had blokes on the jobcentre scheme send me a CV with three years missing and no explanation. It just goes in the bin, sorry, but it does.
Darren: Right. Well, I'd put "back knackered" in mine, so you'd know.
Gemma: That's not what I meant.
Darren: No, I know, I know. It's just everyone's got advice, you know. The work coach, the wife, the bloke in the pub. Sorry, I'm going off on one. It gets to you a bit.
Gemma: ...Yeah. Fair. My dad was a lorry driver. Did his back about four times. He's not great now, health-wise.
Darren: Oh, sorry to hear that. Is he local to you?
Gemma: St Neots. Twenty minutes. I should go more than I do.
Darren: Go when you can, love. Lost my mum six years back, you don't get them back, do you.
Gemma: No. ...Anyway. What's that on your top, Bristol City?
Darren: Bristol City, yeah. Loosely. Bridgwater United properly. You into it?
Gemma: Not really. Husband's Arsenal. I just hear him shouting at the telly.
Darren: Arsenal. Poor sod. There's another bloke in this lot, the computer one, I bet he's Arsenal an' all.
Gemma: He is. I've had him. He was gaming on his lunch break at four o'clock.
Darren: Ha! Good for him, to be fair.
Gemma: I'd have sacked him.
Darren: I bet you would. You've got that look, you have. No offence.
Gemma: None taken. I get it a lot.
Darren: What do you do for fun, then, when you're not sacking people?
Gemma: Walk the dog. Telly. Gin. Tenerife once a year if I can get Craig to book it.
Darren: Tenerife! Been twice. Best holidays I ever had, I'm telling you. Pool, bit of sun, pint at eleven in the morning, nobody looking at you funny—
Gemma: That's it. That's all I want. Sunbed and nobody ringing me abou—

=== CALL C0527 ===
Chloe: Hi! Sorry, hi, can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah. Hi. Craig.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Erm, how are you?
Craig: Fine. Bit knackered. You?
Chloe: Yeah, good, thanks. A bit nervous. I'm always nervous, don't worry, it's not you. Well, it might be a bit you. Sorry, that came out wrong.
Craig: It's fine.
Chloe: ...So, erm, what do you do?
Craig: Software developer. Logistics stuff. You're at uni, yeah?
Chloe: Yeah, how did you know?
Craig: Just a guess. Your room. The cork board.
Chloe: Oh, God, yeah. That's all my placement timetables. I'm doing primary teaching, third year. Last placement soon, so I'm sort of living on that board at the minute.
Craig: Right. My mum was a school receptionist. Primary.
Chloe: Oh, nice! They run the whole place, honestly. Our receptionist on my last placement knew every kid's name, every parent's name, who was allowed to pick up who. Without her the head would've just been stood in the corridor crying.
Craig: Yeah, that sounds like my mum.
Chloe: What's it like, the software stuff? Sorry, I don't really know anything about it.
Craig: It's alright. I sit in a box room and fix things that other people broke. Pays well, so.
Chloe: I bet. Teaching doesn't, really. Everyone keeps telling me that, like I don't know.
Craig: Why do it, then?
Chloe: Erm. Because of the kids, I suppose. It sounds cheesy. But there was a little girl in my Year 4 class who wouldn't come in the door in the mornings, she'd just stand there holding her mum's coat. And by the end of the placement she'd come in and show me her reading book. That was kind of the best thing I've done, if that makes sense.
Craig: Yeah. Fair enough. That's more than I can say for my job.
Chloe: Aw, no, I'm sure it's useful.
Craig: It's useful. It's not that.
Chloe: Mm. Erm, are those gaming headphones?
Craig: Yeah. I play a lot. Probably too much.
Chloe: My brother's the same, he's seventeen. He's up till about three and then my mum's shouting up the stairs. He's doing an electrical apprenticeship with my dad.
Craig: Electrician, your dad?
Chloe: Yeah, self-employed.
Craig: Smart. They earn more than people think. Better than uni, half the time.
Chloe: Oh. Yeah, maybe. I'm the first one in my family to go, so. Bit late now.
Craig: No, I didn't mean you. Mine was a waste of money 'cause I didn't turn up. A 2:2.
Chloe: Oh, that's still good!
Craig: It's alright. Nobody's asked since.
Chloe: Well, that's something. Erm, where are you based?
Craig: Stevenage.
Chloe: Is that near London? Sorry, I'm terrible with—

=== CALL C0528 ===
Chloe: Hi! Sorry, hi. Can you hear me okay?
Gemma: Yeah. Gemma.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Erm, is this your last one as well?
Gemma: Hope so. I've got dinner to sort, well, Craig has.
Chloe: Oh, is that the Craig from the... sorry, no, there's a Craig in this, isn't there?
Gemma: Different Craig. Mine's my husband. Unfortunately for him.
Chloe: Ha. Erm, so what do you do?
Gemma: Warehouse. Site ops manager. You're a student, yeah? Teaching?
Chloe: Yeah! Primary. How did everyone guess that?
Gemma: You look like a teacher. It's the bookshelf.
Chloe: That's fair, actually. They're all picture books. I'm third year, so last placement's coming up, which I'm kind of dreading, to be honest.
Gemma: Why? You'll be fine. It's kids.
Chloe: It's not the kids. It's more being watched. My mentor on my second year one was, erm, quite harsh. She'd sit at the back with a clipboard and then at the end she'd go through everything I'd done wrong, like a list. I sort of went to pieces a bit after one of them. Sorry, that's probably a bit much.
Gemma: No. ...I'm probably that mentor, if I'm honest.
Chloe: Oh no!
Gemma: Well, I am. I'll tell someone it's not good enough in front of their whole shift. Staff don't love me for it.
Chloe: Erm. Does it work, though?
Gemma: Sometimes. Sometimes they just go off sick.
Chloe: Right.
Gemma: You've got to have a thick skin, that's all I'm saying. People will have a go. Doesn't mean you're rubbish.
Chloe: Yeah. That's kind of what my mum says. She's a hairdresser, she gets moaned at all day.
Gemma: There you go. What year d'you want?
Chloe: Key Stage 1, ideally. Year 1 or 2. They're so little, they just tell you everything.
Gemma: My boy's nine. Year 5. Got a letter on the fridge about some Viking day I haven't read yet.
Chloe: Oh, they love a Viking day. You'll probably need a costume.
Gemma: Brilliant. Craig'll do it. He does the school stuff, I'm never there for it. Hours are all over the place.
Chloe: That's really normal, though. Loads of the parents on placement were like that, the dads did drop-off. The kids don't mind, honestly, they just want someone there.
Gemma: Hm. Is that the teacher voice?
Chloe: Sorry, a bit. My dad's an electrician, so he was always the one who could pick us up, 'cause he could fit jobs round it.
Gemma: Craig's a sparky. Self-employed.
Chloe: No way! My dad's self-employed as well. Does he moan about the VAT?
Gemma: Every quarter. Without fail.
Chloe: That's my dad! He goes in the shed and swears at the laptop.
Gemma: That's every electrician in the country, that.
Chloe: Ha. Erm, have you got a dog? I thought I saw one in your photo.
Gemma: Biscuit. Cockapoo. Chewed through my charger this morning, so that's my morning.
Chloe: Aw, ours is a Staffie, she's really old, she just snores on the landi—

=== CALL C0529 ===
Darren: Alright, mate! How you doing?
Bethany: Hi. Erm, good, thanks. I'm Bethany.
Darren: Darren. You look about as done with this as I am.
Bethany: Sorry. No, it's been nice, mostly. I'm just a bit tired.
Darren: Don't apologise, love. Where you calling from?
Bethany: Bridgwater.
Darren: Get away! Me too! Whereabouts?
Bethany: Near the town centre. Above a takeaway, sort of off the main road.
Darren: Not the chippy? With the blue sign?
Bethany: Yeah, that one.
Darren: I've had more cod out of there than I've had hot dinners. Well, they were hot dinners. You know what I mean. Small world, innit. What are the chances, eh?
Bethany: I know. I thought you looked a bit familiar in your photo, actually. Not like I know you. Just... like someone from here.
Darren: It's the face. Everyone in Bridgwater's got the face. You working?
Bethany: Not at the minute. I volunteer at the hospice shop, Tuesdays and Thursdays. I had a packing job but it ended.
Darren: Same boat, me. Back went. Was on the forklifts off the M5 for years.
Bethany: Oh, that's where Kieran works. My boyfriend. He drives forklift there.
Darren: Kieran? Tall lad? Bit quiet?
Bethany: Erm, yeah, quite tall. Quite quiet. Kieran Hollis.
Darren: Might've seen him about. Can't put a face to it, my memory's shot. You tell him Darren says the canteen pasties are a crime.
Bethany: I will. He says that as well.
Darren: Good lad. So what are you after, job-wise?
Bethany: I'm not sure really. Something steady. I sort of thought maybe a garden centre, or the library. But I get really nervous about interviews. I cancelled one once. I just couldn't make myself go.
Darren: Oh, mate, I've done worse. I walked out of one halfway through 'cause the bloke was talking to me like I was thick. Wasn't proud of it. Jobcentre weren't proud of it either.
Bethany: Did you get in trouble?
Darren: Bit of a telling off. Water off a duck's back. Well, sort of. Honestly, though, a library, you'd be brilliant. You've got the library look.
Bethany: That's what someone else said. The Craig one.
Darren: The grumpy one? Don't listen to him. Here, you going carnival this year?
Bethany: Yeah, I go every year. I watch from near the Cornhill, 'cause the crowds are a bit much further down.
Darren: Never missed one. Not once. Last year's winner, though, I'm still not having it. That cart from the year before was miles better, the lights on it—
Bethany: The one with the owls? I drew that one.
Darren: You drew it? Get away. You want to show the club that, they'd—

=== CALL C0530 ===
Gemma: Hi. Gemma. Last one, I think.
Bethany: Hi. Yeah, I think so. I'm Bethany.
Gemma: Right. Go on, then, what do you do?
Bethany: Erm, I'm looking for work at the moment. I did a packing job on a food line, but it was seasonal, so it finished. And I volunteer at a hospice charity shop, two mornings a week.
Gemma: Packing. How long ago did it finish?
Bethany: Erm... just over a year.
Gemma: Right. That's a long gap, you want to watch that. I see CVs every week, and if there's a year with nothing on it, that's the first thing I look at. I'm not saying it's fair. It's just what happens.
Bethany: No, I know. I've put the charity shop on it. And I did a customer service course online, a Level 2.
Gemma: That's something. What were you like on the line?
Bethany: I was alright, I think. I never called in sick. And I always checked the labels twice, 'cause if they're wrong the whole pallet comes back.
Gemma: That's better than half my lot. Honestly, you'd be amazed. I've got pickers who ring in sick 'cause it's raining. You turn up and you check your labels, you'd get a job at mine tomorrow. Well, if you lived nearer. Where are you?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Gemma: Long way from Huntingdon.
Bethany: Yeah. Sorry.
Gemma: Don't be sorry. There's warehouses all down the M5, isn't there.
Bethany: My boyfriend works at one. Kieran. He drives a forklift.
Gemma: There you go, then. Get him to ask. Half my agency staff come in 'cause somebody's mate put a word in. That's how it works, yeah?
Bethany: I hadn't really thought of that. I think I'd sort of like something quieter, though. Like a garden centre, maybe. Or a library.
Gemma: Quiet. Yeah, a warehouse isn't quiet.
Bethany: No. Erm, what's it like, being a manager? It sounds really hard.
Gemma: It's alright. It's long. Fifty, sixty hours some weeks. I was in at six this morning 'cause the agency didn't send enough bodies, then I had a client on the phone screaming about peak, then a trailer that never turned up. You spend all day putting fires out. And people don't like you much, but that's the job, isn't it.
Bethany: I'm sure they like you a bit.
Gemma: Dunno. Never asked. Darren reckons I've got the look.
Bethany: Oh, I talked to him. He lives near me, actually. Same town.
Gemma: Him? He's alright. Reminded me of my dad.
Bethany: He reminded me of my stepdad, a bit.
Gemma: Must be the face. Is that a bird, behind you? On the wall.
Bethany: Yeah, a robin. I drew it. I do birds mostly, and plants. There was a little egret down by the river this morning.
Gemma: Couldn't tell you what an egret is.
Bethany: It's like a small white heron. Sort of. They've got bright yellow feet, like they've stepped in custard.
Gemma: Custard. Right. Put that on your CV, you'd stand out, at lea—

=== CALL C0531 ===
Darren: Here he is! The Arsenal man. Alright, mate?
Craig: Alright. Who told you that?
Darren: Gemma. Said you was gaming on your lunch at four o'clock.
Craig: Course she did. It was a late lunch.
Darren: I'm not judging, mate, I'd do the same. Darren, by the way.
Craig: Craig. You're the forklift one, yeah?
Darren: Was. Back's gone. Eighteen months signed off now. I'm on the Universal Credit, seeing a work coach, all that. Looking at van driving, security, caretaker, anything that doesn't mean twisting round on a counterbalance all day. Honestly, I'd sweep the car park if it paid the rent.
Craig: Right. Have you thought about the office side? Warehouse admin, inventory control. You know the floor, that's half of it. Most of the people doing that have never set foot on a shift.
Darren: Me, in an office? I'd lose the paperwork in a week, mate. I lost paperwork on the forklifts, and that was one sheet.
Craig: They're mostly screens now. Scan it, click it, done.
Darren: Yeah, well. I'm not great on computers.
Craig: Nobody is. That's why I've got a job.
Darren: Ha! Fair. What is it you do, then?
Craig: Write the software warehouses run on. The thing on the scanner that tells you where to go.
Darren: You're joking. So it's you, is it? The one that freezes on a Friday night with forty trailers waiting?
Craig: Probably not me. Usually somebody's put the server in a cupboard.
Darren: Mate, ours was in a cupboard. With the mop.
Craig: There you go.
Darren: Unbelievable. So who's your team, then, apart from Arsenal bottling it?
Craig: That's it. Just Arsenal. Mostly the highlights, if I'm honest.
Darren: Highlights! You're not a fan, you're a viewer. I'm Bristol City, loosely, but Bridgwater United properly. Stood in the rain for them since I was eight.
Craig: Sounds miserable.
Darren: It is. Best thing in the world. You play anything?
Craig: Five-a-side for a bit. The group chat got too organised, so I stopped going.
Darren: Too organised! I've never heard that one. I do darts now, pub team, Thursdays. Back permitting.
Craig: Any good?
Darren: Decent average on a good night. Thursday wasn't a good night. Lost by one leg, and the bloke's double sixteen bounced out and they gave it him anyway.
Craig: How does a bounce-out count?
Darren: It doesn't! That's what I've been saying since Thursday, mate. Nobody'll listen.
Craig: Yeah, that's daft. Get it on video next time.
Darren: See, you're alright, you. Said you looked a grumpy sod in your photo.
Craig: I get that a lot. It's just my face.
Darren: Join the club. What do you do when you're not fixing cupboards, then?
Craig: Gaming. Bit of home server stuff. Smart lights that never quite work.
Darren: Never quite work. I've had a moped in the back yard three years, "nearly finished." Kerry wants it gone.
Craig: Becky says the same about my bike. What's wrong with it?
Darren: Carburettor, I reckon. Or me. Probably me.
Craig: Probably the carb. Send us a picture and I'll—

calls.C0523:
Bethany: Hi. Erm, hello. Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah, fine. Hi.
Bethany: Hi. Sorry, I'm Bethany.
Craig: Craig.
Bethany: ...
Craig: So. Three minutes, yeah?
Bethany: Yeah, I think so. I wasn't sure if we're meant to talk about anything in particular.
Craig: Don't think so. Just chat, I reckon. How'd you get on with the puzzle thing?
Bethany: Erm, not very well, to be honest. I got stuck on the one with the shapes, the rotating ones, and sort of gave up on it in the end.
Craig: Yeah, that one was a bit daft. I just guessed most of them.
Bethany: Oh, that makes me feel a bit better, thanks.
Craig: Where are you, then?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Craig: Right. Never been. Stevenage, me.
Bethany: Oh, okay. Is that near London?
Craig: Sort of. Half an hour on the train. It's fine, yeah. Nothing much there.
Bethany: What do you do? If that's... sorry, if that's okay to ask.
Craig: Yeah, course. Software developer. Back-end stuff, for a logistics company. Basically we write the systems warehouses use, so stock, picking, which lorry goes where, that sort of thing. I mostly work from home, so it's me in the box room all day with the headphones on. Pretty boring to explain, honestly.
Bethany: No, that's quite interesting actually. My boyfriend works in a warehouse. He drives a forklift at a distribution centre off the M5. They've got a system that tells him where to go on a little screen, I think.
Craig: Yeah, that'll be something like ours. Probably not ours, but similar. Does he moan about it?
Bethany: Erm... a bit. He says it freezes sometimes and they all just have to stand around.
Craig: Yeah, that's usually somebody on the back end. Could be me, to be fair.
Bethany: I won't tell him.
Craig: Cheers. What about you, what do you do?
Bethany: Erm, I'm sort of... I'm looking for work at the moment. I did a packing job but it was seasonal, so it ended. I volunteer at a charity shop two mornings a week, the hospice one. So, yeah.
Craig: Fair enough.
Bethany: ...
Craig: Is that your drawing behind you? The bird.
Bethany: Oh, yeah. It's a robin. I draw quite a lot, mostly birds and plants. There's a little egret that's been down by the river this week, so I've been trying to get that, but they don't keep still. They stand dead still for ages and then just go, and you've only got half a leg.
Craig: Half a leg. Yeah, that robin's decent though. Looks proper.
Bethany: Thank you. That's kind.
Craig: You sell them or anything?
Bethany: No, not really. I put some on Instagram. I've got a few hundred followers, which isn't much. I'd like to do commissions maybe, one day, but I'm not sure I'm good enough yet.
Craig: Few hundred's more than I've got. I'd just charge people. Honestly, half of getting paid is just asking for it. I've moved jobs twice 'cause I asked for more money and they said no.
Bethany: I think I'd be too scared to ask.
Craig: Yeah, most people are. That's why they don't get it.
Bethany: Mm. Maybe. Is that a bike behind you? In the corner.
Craig: Yeah. Road bike. Bought it in lockdown, cost way too much. I ride it about four times a year. Needs a service, I've been saying that for about a year.
Bethany: We walk mostly. On the Levels, and up the Quantocks sometimes if Kieran drives us.
Craig: Is that hills?
Bethany: Yeah, sort of... they're not huge, but it's really nice at the top. You can see right over to Wales on a clear day.
Craig: I'd probably cycle it if it was flat.
Bethany: The Levels are flat. Very flat. That's kind of the whole point of them.
Craig: Go on then, maybe I'll stick the bike on the—
calls.C0524:
Gemma: Right. Hi. Can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah. Hi. Craig.
Gemma: Gemma. Funny, my husband's called Craig.
Craig: Lot of us about.
Gemma: Mm. So what is this, we just talk for three minutes and that's it?
Craig: Pretty much. Did one already. Goes quick.
Gemma: Good. I've been on since six, I'm knackered.
Craig: What do you do, then?
Gemma: Site ops manager. Distribution centre up near Alconbury, third-party logistics. About a hundred and eighty staff over three shifts. So basically if a trailer doesn't turn up or the agency don't send enough bodies, it's my phone that goes. Had a client on at me at seven this morning about peak volumes. Peak's a nightmare every year, without fail.
Craig: Huh. I write warehouse software. Logistics company in Cambridge.
Gemma: You're joking.
Craig: Back-end. The bit that works out allocation, picking routes, that sort of thing.
Gemma: Which one?
Craig: Probably not one you'd know. Mid-sized.
Gemma: Well, whoever does ours wants shooting. It goes down every time we hit volume. Every time. Two hundred people stood there with scanners going "Gem, it's frozen again."
Craig: Yeah, that's usually not the software, to be fair.
Gemma: Course it's not.
Craig: No, honestly. Nine times out of ten someone's set it up badly on site. Waves configured wrong, or the server's some ten-year-old box in a comms cupboard. Then they ring us and it's our fault. Had one last month, their whole system was running off a server someone had put a kettle next to.
Gemma: A kettle.
Craig: Steam. In the cupboard. For about two years.
Gemma: ...That's actually quite funny. That'd be my lot an' all, to be honest.
Craig: It's always somebody's lot.
Gemma: Do you go out on site, then, or?
Craig: God, no. Home, mostly. Office once a fortnight.
Gemma: Must be nice. Sat at home in your joggers.
Craig: It's alright, yeah.
Gemma: I'd go mad. I'd also never answer an email again, so. My inbox is about four thousand.
Craig: Four thousand?
Gemma: Ish. My deputy does the important ones, Priya. She's the only reason that place runs, honestly. Don't tell her I said that.
Craig: I'm not gonna meet her.
Gemma: No. Good. ...Cambridge, though, so you're on the A14?
Craig: A1(M). Which is a nightmare.
Gemma: Try the A14. The roadworks. I've spent more time sat by Girton this month than I have at home.
Craig: Yeah, I avoid it.
Gemma: Lucky you. ...Them headphones. You were on a game before this, weren't you?
Craig: Bit. Lunch break.
Gemma: It's gone four.
Craig: Flexible hours.
Gemma: Flexible. Right. If one of my team leaders said that to me I'd have them in the office.
Craig: Good job I don't work for you, then.
Gemma: Yeah, it is, mate. You'd last about a week. My Craig's the same, mind, he's Arsenal, been in a mood since Sunday—
Craig: Oh, don't. They bottled it agai—
calls.C0525:
Chloe: Hiya! Oh, sorry, hi. Can you hear me okay?
Bethany: Yeah. Hi. I'm Bethany.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous, I don't know why, it's only three minutes.
Bethany: No, me too. I've done one already and I still am.
Chloe: Oh, how was it?
Bethany: It was okay. He was nice, sort of. He just didn't say loads. Well, he did, but... I'm not sure really.
Chloe: Oh, I think I know who you mean, from the photos. Erm. Where are you from?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Chloe: Oh, nice. I'm in Bloxwich, which is Walsall, kind of near Birmingham. Probably means nothing to you.
Bethany: Not really, sorry.
Chloe: No, that's fine, it doesn't mean much to anyone! What do you do?
Bethany: I'm looking for work at the moment. I volunteer in a charity shop, the hospice one. What about you?
Chloe: I'm at uni, third year, primary teaching. So I'm about to do my last placement, which I'm kind of terrified about, to be honest. I've done Year 2 and Year 4, and the kids were lovely, it's not the kids. It's more the staff room. Everyone's been there twenty years and they all know where they sit, and you're stood there with your mug like, can I... is this anyone's chair? Sorry, I'm rambling.
Bethany: No, you're not. I'd be scared of the staff room too.
Chloe: It's the worst bit! Honestly, give me thirty six-year-olds any day.
Bethany: Are those picture books behind you?
Chloe: Yeah! I've been collecting them for my classroom, like, when I get one. Some of them are from charity shops, actually. The illustrations in some of them are just gorgeous, the kids stare at them for ages.
Bethany: I love picture books. I sort of draw, a bit. Birds, mostly.
Chloe: Oh, was that your robin? In your photo? I thought that was lovely.
Bethany: Oh. Yeah, that was mine. Thank you. I do pencil and fineliner, mostly what I see by the river or out on the Levels. I'd love to illustrate a nature book one day. Like a proper one, with all the birds in. But I don't know, I'm not really... I'm not sure I'm good enough to call myself an artist. Sorry, that's a bit much.
Chloe: No, it's not! You totally should. Kids would love that. They go mad for birds, honestly. We did a birdwatch in Year 2 and one boy cried because he saw a blue tit.
Bethany: Aw. That's really sweet.
Chloe: He was so happy. Erm, yeah. That's it really.
Bethany: ...
Chloe: Sorry, what else do you like doing?
Bethany: Reading. Walking. And I bake when I can't sleep. I made flapjacks at about two this morning.
Chloe: Oh my God, same. I bake when I'm stressed. I'm doing banana bread tonight for placement prep, but I've got to wait until my mum's done tea.
Bethany: I do banana bread too! Kieran says he's sick of it.
Chloe: Kieran? My brother's called Kieran! He's seventeen, he eats all the crisps.
Bethany: Mine's my boyfriend. He's on nights this week, so it's just me and the smell of chips from downstairs.
Chloe: Chips?
Bethany: We live above a takeaway. It's sort of nice, sometimes, and sometimes it's—
calls.C0526:
Darren: Alright! There she is. Can you hear me, love?
Gemma: Yeah. Gemma.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you. Third one of these for me, I'm getting good at it now.
Gemma: Same. Is this the last one?
Darren: Dunno, mate. I just do what the screen tells me.
Gemma: Fair enough. Where are you?
Darren: Bridgwater, Somerset. Born and bred. You?
Gemma: Huntingdon. Cambridgeshire.
Darren: Never been. Is it nice?
Gemma: It's alright. It's got a Tesco.
Darren: Ha! Sold me. So what do you do, then? You look like you've come straight from work, with the fleece.
Gemma: Yeah, I have. Site ops manager at a distribution centre. Warehouse, basically. About a hundred and eighty staff.
Darren: No way. I was on forklifts, me. Distribution centre off the M5, years. Counterbalance mostly.
Gemma: Yeah? Where are you now, then?
Darren: Er, nowhere at the minute. Did my back in. Signed off about eighteen months ago, so I'm on the Universal Credit, seeing a work coach every couple of weeks, the whole lot. Looking at lighter stuff, van driving maybe, or caretaker at a school. Not much call for a forklift driver who can't twist round, do you know what I mean?
Gemma: Mm. You could do a lot worse than security. We're always short of gatehouse.
Darren: Yeah, that's on the list.
Gemma: Get your CV in early, though, don't wait for it to come to you. I've had blokes on the jobcentre scheme send me a CV with three years missing and no explanation. It just goes in the bin, sorry, but it does.
Darren: Right. Well, I'd put "back knackered" in mine, so you'd know.
Gemma: That's not what I meant.
Darren: No, I know, I know. It's just everyone's got advice, you know. The work coach, the wife, the bloke in the pub. Sorry, I'm going off on one. It gets to you a bit.
Gemma: ...Yeah. Fair. My dad was a lorry driver. Did his back about four times. He's not great now, health-wise.
Darren: Oh, sorry to hear that. Is he local to you?
Gemma: St Neots. Twenty minutes. I should go more than I do.
Darren: Go when you can, love. Lost my mum six years back, you don't get them back, do you.
Gemma: No. ...Anyway. What's that on your top, Bristol City?
Darren: Bristol City, yeah. Loosely. Bridgwater United properly. You into it?
Gemma: Not really. Husband's Arsenal. I just hear him shouting at the telly.
Darren: Arsenal. Poor sod. There's another bloke in this lot, the computer one, I bet he's Arsenal an' all.
Gemma: He is. I've had him. He was gaming on his lunch break at four o'clock.
Darren: Ha! Good for him, to be fair.
Gemma: I'd have sacked him.
Darren: I bet you would. You've got that look, you have. No offence.
Gemma: None taken. I get it a lot.
Darren: What do you do for fun, then, when you're not sacking people?
Gemma: Walk the dog. Telly. Gin. Tenerife once a year if I can get Craig to book it.
Darren: Tenerife! Been twice. Best holidays I ever had, I'm telling you. Pool, bit of sun, pint at eleven in the morning, nobody looking at you funny—
Gemma: That's it. That's all I want. Sunbed and nobody ringing me abou—
calls.C0527:
Chloe: Hi! Sorry, hi, can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah. Hi. Craig.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Erm, how are you?
Craig: Fine. Bit knackered. You?
Chloe: Yeah, good, thanks. A bit nervous. I'm always nervous, don't worry, it's not you. Well, it might be a bit you. Sorry, that came out wrong.
Craig: It's fine.
Chloe: ...So, erm, what do you do?
Craig: Software developer. Logistics stuff. You're at uni, yeah?
Chloe: Yeah, how did you know?
Craig: Just a guess. Your room. The cork board.
Chloe: Oh, God, yeah. That's all my placement timetables. I'm doing primary teaching, third year. Last placement soon, so I'm sort of living on that board at the minute.
Craig: Right. My mum was a school receptionist. Primary.
Chloe: Oh, nice! They run the whole place, honestly. Our receptionist on my last placement knew every kid's name, every parent's name, who was allowed to pick up who. Without her the head would've just been stood in the corridor crying.
Craig: Yeah, that sounds like my mum.
Chloe: What's it like, the software stuff? Sorry, I don't really know anything about it.
Craig: It's alright. I sit in a box room and fix things that other people broke. Pays well, so.
Chloe: I bet. Teaching doesn't, really. Everyone keeps telling me that, like I don't know.
Craig: Why do it, then?
Chloe: Erm. Because of the kids, I suppose. It sounds cheesy. But there was a little girl in my Year 4 class who wouldn't come in the door in the mornings, she'd just stand there holding her mum's coat. And by the end of the placement she'd come in and show me her reading book. That was kind of the best thing I've done, if that makes sense.
Craig: Yeah. Fair enough. That's more than I can say for my job.
Chloe: Aw, no, I'm sure it's useful.
Craig: It's useful. It's not that.
Chloe: Mm. Erm, are those gaming headphones?
Craig: Yeah. I play a lot. Probably too much.
Chloe: My brother's the same, he's seventeen. He's up till about three and then my mum's shouting up the stairs. He's doing an electrical apprenticeship with my dad.
Craig: Electrician, your dad?
Chloe: Yeah, self-employed.
Craig: Smart. They earn more than people think. Better than uni, half the time.
Chloe: Oh. Yeah, maybe. I'm the first one in my family to go, so. Bit late now.
Craig: No, I didn't mean you. Mine was a waste of money 'cause I didn't turn up. A 2:2.
Chloe: Oh, that's still good!
Craig: It's alright. Nobody's asked since.
Chloe: Well, that's something. Erm, where are you based?
Craig: Stevenage.
Chloe: Is that near London? Sorry, I'm terrible with—
calls.C0528:
Chloe: Hi! Sorry, hi. Can you hear me okay?
Gemma: Yeah. Gemma.
Chloe: I'm Chloe. Erm, is this your last one as well?
Gemma: Hope so. I've got dinner to sort, well, Craig has.
Chloe: Oh, is that the Craig from the... sorry, no, there's a Craig in this, isn't there?
Gemma: Different Craig. Mine's my husband. Unfortunately for him.
Chloe: Ha. Erm, so what do you do?
Gemma: Warehouse. Site ops manager. You're a student, yeah? Teaching?
Chloe: Yeah! Primary. How did everyone guess that?
Gemma: You look like a teacher. It's the bookshelf.
Chloe: That's fair, actually. They're all picture books. I'm third year, so last placement's coming up, which I'm kind of dreading, to be honest.
Gemma: Why? You'll be fine. It's kids.
Chloe: It's not the kids. It's more being watched. My mentor on my second year one was, erm, quite harsh. She'd sit at the back with a clipboard and then at the end she'd go through everything I'd done wrong, like a list. I sort of went to pieces a bit after one of them. Sorry, that's probably a bit much.
Gemma: No. ...I'm probably that mentor, if I'm honest.
Chloe: Oh no!
Gemma: Well, I am. I'll tell someone it's not good enough in front of their whole shift. Staff don't love me for it.
Chloe: Erm. Does it work, though?
Gemma: Sometimes. Sometimes they just go off sick.
Chloe: Right.
Gemma: You've got to have a thick skin, that's all I'm saying. People will have a go. Doesn't mean you're rubbish.
Chloe: Yeah. That's kind of what my mum says. She's a hairdresser, she gets moaned at all day.
Gemma: There you go. What year d'you want?
Chloe: Key Stage 1, ideally. Year 1 or 2. They're so little, they just tell you everything.
Gemma: My boy's nine. Year 5. Got a letter on the fridge about some Viking day I haven't read yet.
Chloe: Oh, they love a Viking day. You'll probably need a costume.
Gemma: Brilliant. Craig'll do it. He does the school stuff, I'm never there for it. Hours are all over the place.
Chloe: That's really normal, though. Loads of the parents on placement were like that, the dads did drop-off. The kids don't mind, honestly, they just want someone there.
Gemma: Hm. Is that the teacher voice?
Chloe: Sorry, a bit. My dad's an electrician, so he was always the one who could pick us up, 'cause he could fit jobs round it.
Gemma: Craig's a sparky. Self-employed.
Chloe: No way! My dad's self-employed as well. Does he moan about the VAT?
Gemma: Every quarter. Without fail.
Chloe: That's my dad! He goes in the shed and swears at the laptop.
Gemma: That's every electrician in the country, that.
Chloe: Ha. Erm, have you got a dog? I thought I saw one in your photo.
Gemma: Biscuit. Cockapoo. Chewed through my charger this morning, so that's my morning.
Chloe: Aw, ours is a Staffie, she's really old, she just snores on the landi—
calls.C0529:
Darren: Alright, mate! How you doing?
Bethany: Hi. Erm, good, thanks. I'm Bethany.
Darren: Darren. You look about as done with this as I am.
Bethany: Sorry. No, it's been nice, mostly. I'm just a bit tired.
Darren: Don't apologise, love. Where you calling from?
Bethany: Bridgwater.
Darren: Get away! Me too! Whereabouts?
Bethany: Near the town centre. Above a takeaway, sort of off the main road.
Darren: Not the chippy? With the blue sign?
Bethany: Yeah, that one.
Darren: I've had more cod out of there than I've had hot dinners. Well, they were hot dinners. You know what I mean. Small world, innit. What are the chances, eh?
Bethany: I know. I thought you looked a bit familiar in your photo, actually. Not like I know you. Just... like someone from here.
Darren: It's the face. Everyone in Bridgwater's got the face. You working?
Bethany: Not at the minute. I volunteer at the hospice shop, Tuesdays and Thursdays. I had a packing job but it ended.
Darren: Same boat, me. Back went. Was on the forklifts off the M5 for years.
Bethany: Oh, that's where Kieran works. My boyfriend. He drives forklift there.
Darren: Kieran? Tall lad? Bit quiet?
Bethany: Erm, yeah, quite tall. Quite quiet. Kieran Hollis.
Darren: Might've seen him about. Can't put a face to it, my memory's shot. You tell him Darren says the canteen pasties are a crime.
Bethany: I will. He says that as well.
Darren: Good lad. So what are you after, job-wise?
Bethany: I'm not sure really. Something steady. I sort of thought maybe a garden centre, or the library. But I get really nervous about interviews. I cancelled one once. I just couldn't make myself go.
Darren: Oh, mate, I've done worse. I walked out of one halfway through 'cause the bloke was talking to me like I was thick. Wasn't proud of it. Jobcentre weren't proud of it either.
Bethany: Did you get in trouble?
Darren: Bit of a telling off. Water off a duck's back. Well, sort of. Honestly, though, a library, you'd be brilliant. You've got the library look.
Bethany: That's what someone else said. The Craig one.
Darren: The grumpy one? Don't listen to him. Here, you going carnival this year?
Bethany: Yeah, I go every year. I watch from near the Cornhill, 'cause the crowds are a bit much further down.
Darren: Never missed one. Not once. Last year's winner, though, I'm still not having it. That cart from the year before was miles better, the lights on it—
Bethany: The one with the owls? I drew that one.
Darren: You drew it? Get away. You want to show the club that, they'd—
calls.C0530:
Gemma: Hi. Gemma. Last one, I think.
Bethany: Hi. Yeah, I think so. I'm Bethany.
Gemma: Right. Go on, then, what do you do?
Bethany: Erm, I'm looking for work at the moment. I did a packing job on a food line, but it was seasonal, so it finished. And I volunteer at a hospice charity shop, two mornings a week.
Gemma: Packing. How long ago did it finish?
Bethany: Erm... just over a year.
Gemma: Right. That's a long gap, you want to watch that. I see CVs every week, and if there's a year with nothing on it, that's the first thing I look at. I'm not saying it's fair. It's just what happens.
Bethany: No, I know. I've put the charity shop on it. And I did a customer service course online, a Level 2.
Gemma: That's something. What were you like on the line?
Bethany: I was alright, I think. I never called in sick. And I always checked the labels twice, 'cause if they're wrong the whole pallet comes back.
Gemma: That's better than half my lot. Honestly, you'd be amazed. I've got pickers who ring in sick 'cause it's raining. You turn up and you check your labels, you'd get a job at mine tomorrow. Well, if you lived nearer. Where are you?
Bethany: Bridgwater. In Somerset.
Gemma: Long way from Huntingdon.
Bethany: Yeah. Sorry.
Gemma: Don't be sorry. There's warehouses all down the M5, isn't there.
Bethany: My boyfriend works at one. Kieran. He drives a forklift.
Gemma: There you go, then. Get him to ask. Half my agency staff come in 'cause somebody's mate put a word in. That's how it works, yeah?
Bethany: I hadn't really thought of that. I think I'd sort of like something quieter, though. Like a garden centre, maybe. Or a library.
Gemma: Quiet. Yeah, a warehouse isn't quiet.
Bethany: No. Erm, what's it like, being a manager? It sounds really hard.
Gemma: It's alright. It's long. Fifty, sixty hours some weeks. I was in at six this morning 'cause the agency didn't send enough bodies, then I had a client on the phone screaming about peak, then a trailer that never turned up. You spend all day putting fires out. And people don't like you much, but that's the job, isn't it.
Bethany: I'm sure they like you a bit.
Gemma: Dunno. Never asked. Darren reckons I've got the look.
Bethany: Oh, I talked to him. He lives near me, actually. Same town.
Gemma: Him? He's alright. Reminded me of my dad.
Bethany: He reminded me of my stepdad, a bit.
Gemma: Must be the face. Is that a bird, behind you? On the wall.
Bethany: Yeah, a robin. I drew it. I do birds mostly, and plants. There was a little egret down by the river this morning.
Gemma: Couldn't tell you what an egret is.
Bethany: It's like a small white heron. Sort of. They've got bright yellow feet, like they've stepped in custard.
Gemma: Custard. Right. Put that on your CV, you'd stand out, at lea—
calls.C0531:
Darren: Here he is! The Arsenal man. Alright, mate?
Craig: Alright. Who told you that?
Darren: Gemma. Said you was gaming on your lunch at four o'clock.
Craig: Course she did. It was a late lunch.
Darren: I'm not judging, mate, I'd do the same. Darren, by the way.
Craig: Craig. You're the forklift one, yeah?
Darren: Was. Back's gone. Eighteen months signed off now. I'm on the Universal Credit, seeing a work coach, all that. Looking at van driving, security, caretaker, anything that doesn't mean twisting round on a counterbalance all day. Honestly, I'd sweep the car park if it paid the rent.
Craig: Right. Have you thought about the office side? Warehouse admin, inventory control. You know the floor, that's half of it. Most of the people doing that have never set foot on a shift.
Darren: Me, in an office? I'd lose the paperwork in a week, mate. I lost paperwork on the forklifts, and that was one sheet.
Craig: They're mostly screens now. Scan it, click it, done.
Darren: Yeah, well. I'm not great on computers.
Craig: Nobody is. That's why I've got a job.
Darren: Ha! Fair. What is it you do, then?
Craig: Write the software warehouses run on. The thing on the scanner that tells you where to go.
Darren: You're joking. So it's you, is it? The one that freezes on a Friday night with forty trailers waiting?
Craig: Probably not me. Usually somebody's put the server in a cupboard.
Darren: Mate, ours was in a cupboard. With the mop.
Craig: There you go.
Darren: Unbelievable. So who's your team, then, apart from Arsenal bottling it?
Craig: That's it. Just Arsenal. Mostly the highlights, if I'm honest.
Darren: Highlights! You're not a fan, you're a viewer. I'm Bristol City, loosely, but Bridgwater United properly. Stood in the rain for them since I was eight.
Craig: Sounds miserable.
Darren: It is. Best thing in the world. You play anything?
Craig: Five-a-side for a bit. The group chat got too organised, so I stopped going.
Darren: Too organised! I've never heard that one. I do darts now, pub team, Thursdays. Back permitting.
Craig: Any good?
Darren: Decent average on a good night. Thursday wasn't a good night. Lost by one leg, and the bloke's double sixteen bounced out and they gave it him anyway.
Craig: How does a bounce-out count?
Darren: It doesn't! That's what I've been saying since Thursday, mate. Nobody'll listen.
Craig: Yeah, that's daft. Get it on video next time.
Darren: See, you're alright, you. Said you looked a grumpy sod in your photo.
Craig: I get that a lot. It's just my face.
Darren: Join the club. What do you do when you're not fixing cupboards, then?
Craig: Gaming. Bit of home server stuff. Smart lights that never quite work.
Darren: Never quite work. I've had a moped in the back yard three years, "nearly finished." Kerry wants it gone.
Craig: Becky says the same about my bike. What's wrong with it?
Darren: Carburettor, I reckon. Or me. Probably me.
Craig: Probably the carb. Send us a picture and I'll—

C0530.line_text: Gemma: Right. That's a long gap, you want to watch that. I see CVs every week, and if there's a year with nothing on it, that's the first thing I look at. I'm not saying it's fair. It's just what happens.
C0530.what: While Gemma is talking about the gap on the CV, Bethany's small smile drops. Her eyes go down and to the side, away from the screen, her lips press together, and her shoulders rise and fall in a slow, audible breath out before she looks back up at the camera.
